The stream assembler now keeps at most 200 run states and refreshes insertion order for recently active runs, matching the existing TUI run-bookkeeping ceiling. The file already imports and uses `truncateUtf16Safe` correctly elsewhere (`truncateShortTermSnippet` and `truncatePromotedSnippet`). target.title: [Bug]: Timed-out Codex native hook relays can survive and exhaust memory
target.body:
## Bug type

Crash (process/app exits)

## Beta release blocker

No

## Summary

Timed-out Codex native hook relay commands can leave both the OpenClaw CLI launcher and its detached startup-respawn child alive, allowing relay processes to accumulate until the gateway cgroup exhausts host memory.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Install OpenClaw 2026.7.1 through npm and run the gateway under systemd on Linux with the Codex plugin enabled.
2. Start long-running Codex-backed agent work that emits native hook relay commands. Production commands have the form `nice -n 10 node openclaw.mjs hooks relay ...` and Codex 0.144.3 applies a 10-second command-hook timeout.
3. Under load, inspect the process tree while a relay starts. The shell owns an OpenClaw launcher, and startup respawn creates a detached `openclaw-hooks` child in a new process group/session.
4. Let Codex's hook timeout expire or kill the shell/launcher PID to model its `kill_on_drop` behavior.
5. Observe that the detached relay child remains alive. Repeating timed-out hook starts accumulates relay processes.

A deterministic local process-tree check reproduced the ownership break: before cancellation there was an OpenClaw launcher plus a detached `openclaw-hooks` child; killing the timeout-owned launcher did not terminate the detached child.

## Expected behavior

The Codex hook timeout should own and terminate the actual relay Node process, and `openclaw hooks relay` should not create a detached startup-respawn child.

## Actual behavior

At 2026-07-16 21:24 UTC, a kernel OOM snapshot contained 19 `openclaw-hooks` processes using 3.84 GiB RSS plus 30 `openclaw` launcher/startup processes using 2.56 GiB RSS, for 49 processes and approximately 6.40 GiB aggregate RSS. The kernel killed the OpenClaw gateway after earlier memory-pressure kills.

The OpenClaw service recorded a 6.38 GiB memory peak and 287 tasks. Individual relay workers were observed at roughly 200-490 MiB. `OPENCLAW_NO_RESPAWN=1` materially reduces this failure mode but should not be required for an internal relay command.

The process chain is:

1. Codex runs the hook string through `/bin/sh -lc` and kills only that direct child when the timeout future is dropped.
2. The generated `nice ...` command remains a shell child unless the command uses `exec`.
3. OpenClaw startup respawn detaches its adjusted-Node-options child for noninteractive CLI commands.
4. The timeout therefore loses ownership of the memory-heavy relay process.

## OpenClaw version

2026.7.1 (2d2ddc4)

## Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, Linux 6.8.0-111-generic, x86_64

## Install method

npm global; systemd user service

## Model

openai/gpt-5.6-sol

## Provider / routing chain

OpenClaw -> bundled Codex app-server (`@openai/codex` 0.144.3) -> OpenAI

## Additional provider/model setup details

Codex plugin enabled with the default native hook relay settings. Gateway service is supervised by systemd. The service-level `OPENCLAW_NO_RESPAWN=1` setting is a confirmed mitigation, but the internal command currently relies on that external environment to avoid the detached respawn.

## Logs

```shell
# systemd peak from the affected service lifetime
MemoryPeak=6854258688
TasksMax=9483

# Kernel OOM task snapshot totals at 21:24 UTC
openclaw-hooks: 19 processes, 1006284 RSS pages, 3.84 GiB
openclaw launchers: 30 processes, 670403 RSS pages, 2.56 GiB
combined: 49 processes, 1676687 RSS pages, 6.40 GiB
```

Gateway logs also contained repeated `native hook relay not found` errors. Those late relay lookup failures appear adjacent but are not required to reproduce the process ownership bug described here.

## Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Source inspection against the bundled Codex tag confirms its hook runner uses `/bin/sh -lc`, `kill_on_drop(true)`, and a Tokio timeout around `wait_with_output`; it does not terminate a process group. OpenClaw's startup respawn path uses `detached: true` for noninteractive commands.

## Impact and severity

Affected systems: Linux OpenClaw gateways using the Codex native hook relay, especially shared hosts running overlapping long agent jobs.

Severity: High. The observed consequence is host-wide memory pressure followed by kernel OOM kills of unrelated services and finally the OpenClaw gateway.

Frequency: Intermittent under ordinary load, but repeatable when relay startup exceeds the Codex hook timeout. Once the host is under pressure, slower relay startup makes further accumulation more likely.

Consequence: Failed support/onboarding work, gateway restart, stranded processes, and collateral OOM kills.

## Additional information

Proposed narrow fix:

- Prefix POSIX relay commands with `exec` so Codex's timeout-owned shell PID becomes the relay process.
- Exempt the internal `hooks relay` command from OpenClaw's startup environment respawn policy so it cannot detach a replacement child.
- Remove `OPENCLAW_NO_RESPAWN=1` from relay lifecycle tests and add explicit command/policy regression coverage.

Related but not duplicate: #73723 and its follow-up fixes cover missing relay registration and late unregister races. This report is specifically about relay subprocess ownership after timeout.

target.title: Bound HTTP error body snippets to readable streams
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readResponseBodySnippet` was meant to produce a bounded diagnostic snippet for upstream HTTP error responses, but its body-less fallback used whole-body response methods before truncating. A response without a usable `ReadableStream.getReader()` could still force the process to materialize the entire error body just to produce a short snippet.

## Why This Change Was Made

This keeps the streamed path on `readResponseTextPrefix`, which already enforces the byte cap and cancels overflow, and fails closed for body-less/non-readable responses by returning an empty snippet instead of calling `text()` or `arrayBuffer()`. Without a readable stream there is no cancellable bounded prefix reader, so skipping the diagnostic body is safer than whole-body buffering.

## User Impact

Oversized upstream error bodies can no longer bypass the diagnostic snippet byte cap through the body-less fallback. Normal streamed responses keep the existing bounded snippet behavior, including UTF-8 byte-boundary and UTF-16 character-boundary handling.

## Evidence

**Scope:** 2 files (production `src/infra/http-error-body.ts` +1/-10, test `src/infra/http-error-body.test.ts` +39/-125).

**Changes:**
- Source: -9 net (removes whole-body fallback, returns empty string for body-less responses)
- Tests: -86 net (replaces fallback-oriented tests with stream and failure coverage)

**Local test execution:**
- ✅ `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/http-error-body.test.ts` — 7 tests passed (375ms)
- ✅ `git diff --check -- src/infra/http-error-body.ts src/infra/http-error-body.test.ts` — no whitespace/formatting issues

**CI status:**
- ✅ `auto-response` — passed
- ✅ `Real behavior proof` — passed
- ✅ `actionlint` — passed
- ✅ `Workflow Sanity` — passed

**Live behavior proof (executed July 17, 2026):**

```bash
$ node scripts/demo-http-error-body.mjs

=== LIVE PROOF: HTTP Error Body Snippet Demonstration ===

Test 1: Body-less response (no readable stream)
Response without readable stream:
  - response.body = null
  - Calling text() or arrayBuffer() would throw

Result AFTER fix:
  - Snippet: "" (empty string, as expected)
  - text() called: NO ✅
  - arrayBuffer() called: NO ✅
  - Process did not buffer entire body: YES ✅

Test 2: Streamed response within limits
Raw response: {"error":"authentication failed"}
Snippet result: {"error":"authentication failed"}
  - Stream path works: YES ✅
  - UTF-8 text decoded correctly: YES ✅

Test 3: Large response truncated by byte limit
Raw response: 500 bytes of 'a'
```

target.title: fix(plugins): plugins.deny is bypassed by a mixed-case manifest id
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators who denylist a plugin would still have that plugin load in full, when the plugin's manifest declares its id in a different case than the denylist entry.

Plugin config policy lists are lowercase-normalized: `plugins.deny`, `plugins.allow`, and `plugins.entries` keys all pass through `normalizePluginId`, which trims and lowercases. A plugin's self-declared manifest id is only trimmed. So when an operator denylists `malicious-scraper` and a plugin publishes `"id": "Malicious-Scraper"`, the denylist comparison misses, no diagnostic is emitted, and the plugin falls through to default activation with its hooks, channels, secret provider integrations, tools, and services loaded. The operator sees the plugin listed as enabled with no indication their denylist entry did nothing.

The same gap applies to the core reserved-id check: a manifest declaring `"id": "Node-MCP"` evades the `CORE_RESERVED_PLUGIN_IDS` rejection that `node-mcp` would hit.

The allowlist side of the mismatch fails closed rather than open: a legitimately allowlisted plugin that declares a mixed-case id is blocked as `not-in-allowlist`.

## Why This Change Was Made

The two sides of each policy comparison are in different cases. `src/plugins/manifest.ts` mints `PluginManifestRecord.id` with a trim-only normalizer, while `src/plugins/config-state.ts` normalizes every config-side id with `normalizeOptionalLowercaseString`. The consumers that mismatch:

- `src/plugins/manifest-owner-policy.ts:57` — `normalizedConfig.deny.includes(params.plugin.id)`
- `src/plugins/config-activation-shared.ts:161` — `params.config.deny.includes(params.id)`

This change derives a lowercase **policy key** at each enforcement boundary and compares that, leaving the manifest-declared id untouched:

```ts
// src/plugins/plugin-policy-id.ts
export function normalizePluginPolicyId(id: string): string {
  return normalizeOptionalLowercaseString(id) ?? "";
}
```

```ts
// src/plugins/manifest-owner-policy.ts
const policyId = normalizePluginPolicyId(params.plugin.id);
if (params.normalizedConfig.deny.includes(policyId)) {
  return "blocked-by-denylist";
}
```

This fixes the denylist check, the allowlist check, the per-entry `enabled: false` check, and the reserved-id check.

### Why not canonicalize the manifest id itself (changed since the last review)

The previous revision of this PR lowercased `PluginManifestRecord.id` at the parse boundary. **That approach is not upgrade-safe, and the review that flagged it was correct.** `record.id` is also matched against the plugin's *runtime export* id, and a mismatch is a hard load failure, not a warning:

- `src/plugins/loader-cli-registry.ts:253` — `if (definition?.id && definition.id !== record.id)` → `plugin id mismatch (config uses "…", export uses "…")`
- `src/plugins/loader-channel-runtime.ts:146,194` — same check for runtime entry and runtime export
- these route to `pushPluginValidationError` (`src/plugins/loader-shared.ts:259`), which sets `status: "error"` and skips registration

Nothing lowercases the runtime export id (`definePluginEntry` returns `id` verbatim). So an existing third-party plugin that declares `"My-Plugin"` in **both** its manifest and its runtime export would load today and stop loading after upgrade. Deriving a policy key avoids that break entirely: identity is preserved, only the comparison is canonicalized.

Alias mapping deliberately stays out of this path. `normalizePluginId` also resolves legacy config aliases, which is an input-normalization concern for operator-typed config, not for policy comparison.

Slots (`plugins.slots.memory` / `contextEngine`) are intentionally left comparing the declared id, because slot values are trimmed but not lowercased config-side; changing that would be a separate behavior change.

## User Impact

Operators who denylist a plugin now have that denylist honored regardless of the case the plugin author chose for its manifest id. A plugin can no longer self-select out of `plugins.deny` by publishing a mixed-case id, and cannot claim a mixed-case spelling of a core reserved id.

All 59 manifest ids shipped in this repo are already lowercase, so this is a no-op for every bundled plugin. Config-side behavior is untouched. Plugin identity is unchanged, so no installed plugin changes id or stops loading.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof: live Gateway runtime inspection, before and after

Both captures drive the real Gateway plugin bootstrap (`loadPluginLookUpTable()` → `loadGatewayStartupPlugins()`) against **the same base**, pristine `main` at `3da3318c56f`, with two on-disk bundled plugins and identical inputs. The only difference is the patch.

Fixture: manifest id `Denied-Fixture` and `Allowed-Fixture`, each with a **runtime export declaring the same mixed-case id** (the upgrade case). Config: `deny: ["denied-fixture"]`, no allowlist. Both register a legacy hook, typed Gateway hook, tool, channel, service, and secret-provider integration.

**BEFORE — pristine main `3da3318c56f`: the denylist does nothing**

```json
{
  "config": { "deny": ["denied-fixture"] },
  "deniedRecord": { "id": "Denied-Fixture", "enabled": true, "status": "loaded",
                    "reason": "bundled default enablement" },
  "runtimeSurfaces": {
    "imported":           ["Allowed-Fixture", "Denied-Fixture"],
    "hooks":              ["Allowed-Fixture", "Denied-Fixture", "Allowed-Fixture", "Denied-Fixture"],
    "tools":              ["Allowed-Fixture", "Denied-Fixture"],
    "channels":           ["Allowed-Fixture", "Denied-Fixture"],
    "services":           ["Allowed-Fixture", "Denied-Fixture"],
    "secretIntegrations": ["Allowed-Fixture", "Denied-Fixture"]
  }
}
```

**AFTER — same base `3da3318c56f` + this patch: denied contributes nothing, control still loads**

```json
{
  "config": { "deny": ["denied-fixture"] },
  "deniedRecord":  { "id": "Denied-Fixture",  "enabled": false, "status": "disabled",
                     "reason": "blocked by denylist" },
  "allowedRecord": { "id": "Allowed-Fixture", "enabled": true,  "status": "loaded",
                     "reason": "bundled default enablement" },
  "runtimeSurfaces": {
    "imported":           ["Allowed-Fixture"],
    "hooks":              ["Allowed-Fixture", "Allowed-Fixture"],
    "tools":              ["Allowed-Fixture"],
    "channels":           ["Allowed-Fixture"],
    "services":           ["Allowed-Fixture"],
    "secretIntegrations": ["Allowed-Fixture"]
  }
}
```

The denied mixed-case plugin is rejected before runtime registration: its record reads `blocked by denylist` and it contributes no imported runtime, hook, tool, channel, service, or secret-integration surface. `Allowed-Fixture` — a mixed-case manifest whose runtime export declares the **same** mixed-case id — still loads with every surface intact and keeps its declared identity, which is the upgrade regression the previous review asked for.

### Correction to the previous revision's Gateway fixture

The earlier fixture did not actually exercise this bug, and its snapshot was not evidence of the fix. Two confounders, both found by running it against pristine main:

1. **It set `allow: ["allowed-fixture"]`.** A non-empty allowlist scopes plugin *discovery* by a lowercased id, so `Denied-Fixture` was dropped before policy ever compared its manifest id. On pristine main the denied plugin was already absent from the registry — for the wrong reason.
2. **Its plugin directories were named in lowercase**, so discovery could match the deny entry by directory name rather than manifest id.

It also exported a lowercase runtime id against a mixed-case manifest, which is why it never surfaced the identity-contract break above. The fixture now names directories after the declared id, drops the allowlist so `deny` is the thing under test, and exports the matching mixed-case runtime id. Verified failing against pristine main and passing with the patch.

### Validation

- `src/gateway/server-plugin-bootstrap.browser-plugin.integration.test.ts` — 2 passed (Gateway bootstrap, denied/allowed surface proof).
- `src/plugins/plugin-policy-id.test.ts` — 7 passed: declared identity preserved, lowercase ids unchanged, deny blocking via owner policy and via the shared activation decision, allow matching, per-entry disable, mixed-case reserved id rejected.
- `src/plugins/manifest-owner-policy.test.ts` — passes unchanged.
- `tsc --noEmit`: clean. `oxlint` shards: clean. `oxfmt`: clean.
- Broad `vitest run src/plugins/` on this Windows dev machine has substantial pre-existing failures unrelated to this change; the patched tree is strictly better than the baseline (main: 91 failed files / 555 failed tests; patched: 88 / 519). CI remains the authority.

Branch base: `3ca2ea71a40`. Current head: `c181d8fadb7`.

target.title: Manage Claw cron jobs through the gateway
target.body:
## Summary

- install grouped Claw cron declarations through the gateway-owned `cron.add` API
- persist pending, complete, failed, or removed ownership references keyed by final agent id and declaration id
- expose cron ownership in status, round-trip complete declarations through export, and include exact cron state in remove consent
- disable Claw-owned recurring work before canonical agent deletion, package cleanup, or workspace cleanup
- reuse and extend the canonical agent deletion lifecycle without letting Claws delete unrelated agent files

## Contract

- scheduler mutation stays in the gateway; Claws never write the cron store directly
- declaration keys are scoped as `claw:<agent-id>:<manifest-job-id>`, so package-local ids do not collide globally
- response-lost retries reconcile by declaration key before issuing another `cron.add`
- `main` declarations target `session:agent:<final-agent-id>:main`; `isolated` remains isolated, and strict v1 validation rejects other session modes
- removal calls `cron.remove` before any agent/config mutation and records partial state if recurring work cannot be proven disabled
- canonical `agents.delete` remains responsible for normal agent cleanup; Claws request config/session cleanup while retaining their narrowly managed workspace files for digest-aware removal

## Stack

- RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27
- Depends on: #102306 grouped export
- This PR: gateway-owned cron mutation, provenance, status, export, and removal
- Next: #102406 validated MCP ownership

All behavior remains gated by `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1`.

## Validation

- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.test.src.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/test-src.tsbuildinfo`
- 61 focused cron/lifecycle/schema/provenance/export unit tests
- 15 Claws CLI tests
- 11 canonical agent-delete command tests
- 1 shared agent-cron cleanup test
- 96 gateway agent-mutation tests across gateway projects
- 8 full lifecycle CLI E2E tests
- emitted `cron.add` payload validated by the gateway protocol validator
- Oxlint: 0 warnings, 0 errors across 18 code/generated files
- Oxfmt: all 18 files correctly formatted
- `git diff --check`
- Codex review: no accepted/actionable findings

## Real behavior proof

The lifecycle tests prove consent-bound add, scheduler-id provenance, response-lost reconciliation, status/export visibility, and removal ordering. A scheduler failure returns partial with `agentRemoved: false`; successful removal calls `cron.remove` before either direct config mutation or the canonical agent-delete delegate.

target.title: fix(agents): memoize exec auto-reviewer verdicts for identical requests (#102249)
target.body:
## Summary

- Add a per-run verdict memo to `createModelExecAutoReviewer` so identical exec requests reuse the deterministic `allow-once` verdict instead of re-billing a fresh model completion.
- Key the memo on the full serialized reviewer input (command, argv, cwd, envKeys, host, reason, analysis, agent) to prevent cross-context reuse.

## What Problem This Solves

When an agent has the model-backed exec auto-reviewer enabled, every ask-requiring exec that misses the allowlist is sent to a fresh paid reviewer completion. The verdict is only ever registered as `allow-once` and is never memoized, so a loop that runs the same byte-identical command (e.g. `npm test`) pays for one reviewer completion per invocation. N identical execs cost N paid reviewer calls.

## User Impact

- **Why it matters / User impact:** Agents running repeated commands in loops (poll/retry patterns, `npm test` iterations) no longer burn redundant paid reviewer completions. Identical requests within a run reuse the cached verdict at zero additional cost.
- **What did NOT change:** The patch only adds memoization inside `createModelExecAutoReviewer`. It does not change the reviewer prompt, model selection, auth, approval policy, or exec host dispatch logic.
- **Architecture / source-of-truth check:** The memo uses the same serialized input that `stringifyInput` sends to the model, ensuring the cached verdict is only reused when the reviewer would see an identical prompt.

## Origin / follow-up

Fixes #102249. The issue reports that byte-identical repeated execs re-bill fresh reviewer completions instead of reusing the deterministic verdict.

target.title: fix(cron): support current and session: targets in initial delivery resolution
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`resolveInitialCronDelivery` in `src/cron/service/initial-delivery.ts` only checks `sessionTarget === "isolated"` when deciding whether to inject default `{ mode: "announce" }` delivery. All other cron code paths already treat `"isolated"`, `"current"`, and `"session:"` as equivalent for this purpose, creating an inconsistency.

## Why This Change Was Made

After #98947 restored persistent session targets, the three sessionTarget values are treated identically in:
- `delivery-plan.ts:106-114` — `isDetachedOutputJob` check
- `normalize.ts:680-684` — `isDetachedDeliveryJob` check
- `jobs.ts:288-298` — `isIsolatedLike` check

But `initial-delivery.ts` was not updated, so cron jobs created with `--session-target current` or `--session-target session:...` would not get the default announce delivery at creation time.

## User Impact

Users creating cron jobs with `sessionTarget: "current"` or `"session:"` may miss delivery announcements.

## Evidence

**Exact head:** `afceffd830f0df94e315326ff8854e3ce99c19a8`

**End-to-end behavior proof (real gateway from the worktree at exact head, repo mock OpenAI, bundled `qa-channel` + in-repo QA bus; isolated `HOME`/`OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`/`OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`; no real credentials):** for BOTH `current` and `session:*` targets — CLI `cron add` creation → persisted delivery state (`cron list --json` + SQLite `cron_jobs`: `delivery_mode=announce`, `delivery_channel=last`) → `cron run` execution (the `session:*` job ran inside the persistent session `agent:main:qa-channel:channel:channel:qa-room`) → exactly one observed announcement per job delivered to the session channel (`qa-channel:channel:qa-room`). Full redacted transcripts: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/99115#issuecomment-4985152103

**Regression coverage placement:** the direct-service contract is now documented in `src/cron/service/initial-delivery.ts` (supported creation paths fill delivery in `normalizeCronJobCreate`; this helper governs direct-service `CronService.add`/declarative-convergence callers and stays consistent with `src/cron/normalize.ts` + `src/cron/delivery-plan.ts`), with caller-level tests through the public `CronService.add` contract added in `src/cron/service/initial-delivery.test.ts`.

**Validation (exact head):**
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cron/service/initial-delivery.test.ts --run`: 16/16 passed
- Neighboring cron suites (`normalize.test.ts`, `service.jobs.test.ts`, `service.declarative-jobs.test.ts`, `delivery-plan.test.ts`): 145/145 passed

target.body:
## Summary

- add experimental `claws export <agent-id> --out <new-directory>`
- project one installed agent into the grouped portable Claw schema
- copy ledger-managed workspace files and safe workspace-relative avatars into package sidecars
- always assign regenerated exports a derivative package identity and content-derived version
- omit nonportable remote avatars, normalize empty optional arrays, and expand `~` in output paths

## Scope

Export reads the provenance established by the add/status lifecycle and writes a new self-contained package without mutating the installed Claw. It accepts an exact agent id, explicitly projects portable agent fields, copies only ledger-managed workspace files plus a validated local avatar, emits exact recorded package references, and refuses unavailable managed files or an existing output directory.

Image data avatars remain inline. A safe local avatar is read through the pinned workspace avatar boundary, copied under `workspace/`, and rewritten to a workspace-relative manifest path. Remote, missing, or unsafe local avatars are omitted because they are not portable package state.

Every regenerated package is emitted as `openclaw-claw-<agent-id>@0.0.0-export.<content-hash>`, including an unchanged installation. Export never reuses an authenticated publisher's package name/version unless it can return the byte-for-byte original artifact, which this command intentionally does not do.

This slice emits the schema's JSON-compatible representation. The later dedicated #106888 slice changes the canonical exported representation to `CLAW.md` while preserving this package and round-trip behavior.

## Stack

- RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27
- Depends on: #102296 status/remove and ownership-aware lifecycle state
- This PR: portable creation/export experience
- Next: #102383 gateway-owned cron lifecycle
- Canonical `CLAW.md`: #106888

## Validation

- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.test.src.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/test-src.tsbuildinfo`
- Oxlint: 0 warnings, 0 errors across all 6 PR files
- Oxfmt: all 6 PR files correctly formatted
- 8 export unit tests
- 15 Claws CLI tests
- 8 full lifecycle E2E tests
- `git diff --check`
- Codex review: no accepted/actionable findings

## Real behavior proof

target.title: fix(agents): bound IDENTITY.md reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` loaded `IDENTITY.md` with `fs.readFileSync(..., "utf-8")` and no size cap. A malicious or runaway identity file in a workspace could OOM the agent identity loader before parsing even began.

## Why This Change Was Made

Identity files are small human-authored markdown, so the existing shared workspace bootstrap cap (`MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES`, 2 MiB, exported from `src/agents/workspace.ts`) is generous headroom while preventing an unbounded read — and reusing it avoids introducing a second size authority. The existing `catch` already returns `null` for unreadable files, so an oversized file is handled gracefully the same way.

## User Impact

- Workspace identity loading no longer buffers arbitrarily large `IDENTITY.md` files.
- Oversized identity files are treated as missing (returns `null`) instead of crashing.
- Normal identity files work exactly as before.

## Evidence

Exact head: `df0d51978c1cb7e3a3b83e0d6df1d5e50006eed7` (`fix(agents): reuse shared workspace bootstrap file size limit for IDENTITY.md`).

- `loadIdentityFromFile` in `src/agents/identity-file.ts` now reads via `readRegularFileSync({ filePath, maxBytes: MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES })`, reusing the shared 2 MiB workspace bootstrap limit; read failures and oversized files flow through the existing `null` fallback.
- Regression tests in `src/agents/identity-file.test.ts` cover a normal load and an oversized file at `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES + 1`.

### Standalone terminal proof (exact head, outside Vitest)

A Node/tsx script imports the changed loader (`loadAgentIdentityFromWorkspace`) and the shared limit directly from source at this head, then exercises a normal file, a file exactly at the 2 MiB cap, and a file one byte over the cap in a throwaway `/tmp` workspace (fixtures deleted after the run; private paths redacted):

```text
$ node -v && git rev-parse HEAD
v24.15.0
df0d51978c1cb7e3a3b83e0d6df1d5e50006eed7

$ tsx proof-101447.mjs
MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES = 2097152 (2 MiB)

=== Normal IDENTITY.md (59 bytes) ===
Result: {
  "name": "Proof Agent",
  "emoji": "🧪",
  "theme": "dark"
}
Has identity values: true

=== IDENTITY.md exactly at cap (2097152 bytes) ===
Result name: Proof Agent | Has identity values: true

=== Oversized IDENTITY.md (2097153 bytes = cap + 1) ===
loadAgentIdentityFromWorkspace result: null
Treated as missing (returns null): true
readRegularFileSync threw: File exceeds 2097152 bytes: <tmp-workspace>/IDENTITY.md

Removed temp workspace. Standalone proof complete.
```

The oversized file (2 MiB + 1, larger than `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES`) is rejected by the bounded reader with `File exceeds 2097152 bytes`, and the loader returns `null` — the agent falls back to no custom identity instead of buffering the file. Files at or under the cap load and parse exactly as before.

### Focused regression tests (exact head)

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/identity-file.test.ts --run
[test] starting test/vitest/vitest.agents.config.ts

 RUN  v4.1.9 <worktree>

 ✓ |agents| src/agents/identity-file.test.ts (10 tests) 299ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  10 passed (10)
   Duration  2.67s

[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 9.75s
```

This includes `returns null when IDENTITY.md exceeds the size cap`, which writes `MAX_WORKSPACE_BOOTSTRAP_FILE_BYTES + 1` bytes and asserts the `null` fallback.

target.title: fix(memory-core): use surrogate-safe UTF-16 slicing in short-term promotion
target.body:
Fixes #107876.

## What Problem This Solves

`extensions/memory-core/src/short-term-promotion.ts` sliced strings at fixed UTF-16 code-unit boundaries without regard to surrogate pairs.

1. Line 417 used `withoutPrefix.slice(0, 200)`; if the 200th code unit was the high surrogate of an astral character (e.g., emoji), the resulting `head` ended with a lone surrogate.
2. Line 2108 used `targetSnippet.slice(0, bodyIndex)`; if `bodyIndex` landed inside a surrogate pair, the slice contained a dangling surrogate half.

## Why This Change Was Made

The file already imports and uses `truncateUtf16Safe` correctly elsewhere (`truncateShortTermSnippet` and `truncatePromotedSnippet`). Using the existing surrogate-safe helpers at the two remaining sites makes the behavior consistent and prevents malformed Unicode strings from reaching downstream regex tests, JSON serialization, SQLite storage, or logging.

## User Impact

Short-term promotion snippets that contain astral characters (emoji, CJK extension characters, math symbols, etc.) near the 200-code-unit lead boundary are now handled without producing lone surrogates.

## Evidence

### Regression coverage

Added two focused tests to the existing `UTF-16 snippet bounds` block in `extensions/memory-core/src/short-term-promotion.test.ts`. Both exercise the modified paths through public functions without exporting internal helpers, and both assert concrete outcomes:

- `does not throw when the dreaming narrative lead window contains an astral character` — records a recall whose snippet has 199 ASCII chars plus 🚀, forcing the 200th code unit to land inside the emoji (the exact surrogate boundary). Ranking exercises the `truncateUtf16Safe(withoutPrefix, 200)` path and returns one candidate because the `Candidate:` marker starts after the lead window.
- `does not throw when heading context contains an astral character` — records a daily recall whose heading and snippet contain 🚀, then asserts `rankShortTermPromotionCandidates` returns one candidate with key `memory:memory/2026-05-28.md:4:4`.

### Exact-boundary runtime proof

Ran a standalone script against the real production module that shows the split surrogate produced by the old raw slice and the well-formed output produced by the patched code, then exercises both real memory-core ranking paths.

Command used:

```bash

export OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=$(mktemp -d)
node_modules/.bin/tsx utf16-exact-boundary-proof.mjs
```

```text
Input length (code units): 269
Input ends with emoji at boundary: yes

Old raw slice (would produce split surrogate):

  rawHead1 last code unit: d83d
  rawHead1 lone surrogate: YES

Real production path after fix:

  safeSlice2 lone surrogate: no

All exact-boundary assertions passed.
```

## Summary

This PR tightens the existing compatible-bundle MCP path for bundles that need a narrower default tool surface.

- Adds regression coverage that a Codex-compatible bundle `.mcp.json` preserves `toolFilter.include`, `toolFilter.exclude`, and a relative bundle data root.
- Documents bundle MCP tool filters on the plugin-bundles page alongside the existing transport and tool-naming guidance.
- Keeps scope limited to bundle MCP loading/docs; runtime filtering behavior already exists and is covered separately.

Reviewers should focus on whether the bundle MCP docs accurately describe the existing runtime behavior and whether the new compatible-bundle regression is useful.

## Linked context

No issue filed.

Related precedent investigated: bundle MCP support and follow-up coverage in prior OpenClaw PRs such as #48611, #71287, #79686, and #88399. This PR follows that existing bundle MCP seam.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

Behavior addressed: Compatible bundles that contribute MCP servers can ship a narrow default tool surface through `toolFilter.include` and `toolFilter.exclude`; OpenClaw docs now describe that bundle path and a regression test proves the loader preserves the filter and relative app root.

Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw checkout on macOS, branch `test/filtered-bundle-mcp`, commit `d5bffb3dc0`, with an isolated temporary `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_HOME`, and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`.

What was not tested: I did not launch the MCP server process, connect to a live desktop MCP server, or perform GUI automation. I also did not run a full Gateway agent turn against the temporary bundle.

Proof limitations or environment constraints: The proof uses a temporary local compatible bundle and the real OpenClaw plugin installer/loader, but the MCP server command itself is not started because this PR changes documentation and loader regression coverage, not MCP runtime execution behavior.

## Files touched
- `extensions/memory-core/index.ts` — lazy `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptors
- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts` — concrete `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptions
- `extensions/memory-core/src/prompt-section.ts` — system-prompt recall guidance

## Note

target.title: refactor(gateway-client): expose request dispatch boundary
target.body:
Related: #96230

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway-internal callers can observe a request result or a later `accepted` response, but cannot distinguish a failure before the request frame entered the local WebSocket transport from a failure after dispatch. That distinction is required before later restart-recovery work can make conservative retry or refund decisions without guessing from promise settlement.

This is the first independently reviewable dependency extracted from #96230. The original PR remains frozen while its behavior is split into ordered, narrower changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The protocol client is the only layer that owns the synchronous `socket.send(...)` boundary, so this adds an optional `onDispatched` observer immediately after `send` returns successfully and routes it through the existing callback-isolation helper. The package client and high-level `callGateway` wrapper forward the same observer without changing request frames, protocol versions, timeout/abort cleanup, reconnect behavior, or `onAccepted` response semantics.

The observer contract is intentionally narrow: it means the request frame was handed to the local WebSocket transport. It does not mean the Gateway/server accepted or processed the request. The request option type lives in a dedicated small module and is re-exported from the existing protocol-client module, preserving import and structural type compatibility. `GatewayClient` forwards that shared option shape as a unit, then overrides only its normalized `expectFinal` and `timeoutMs` values; this keeps the oversized implementation LOC-neutral without deleting unrelated comments.

This is a root-cause boundary fix: higher layers no longer need to infer whether transport dispatch happened. The gateway-client package is private and the new field is additive and optional. A consumer/test-double sweep covered the package export, OpenClaw facade, SDK transport, accepted-response caller, both affected request stubs, and the node-host bridge. The node-host bridge only forwards `timeoutMs` across its IPC boundary, so later recovery code must use `callGateway` or introduce a separate IPC dispatch acknowledgement rather than assuming this observer is available there.

Out of scope for this PR: Plugin SDK/session-state isolation, recovery persistence, `mainRestartRecovery` admission or ownership, bounded recovery, quarantine, and Doctor repair. In particular, this PR does not write any production recovery state.

## User Impact

There is no direct end-user behavior change. Existing callers behave exactly as before; later recovery PRs can use a precise local transport-dispatch fact instead of broad failure inference.

Risk is limited to an additive observer callback. It is not invoked when WebSocket send throws, observer exceptions are isolated from request settlement, and the callback must not be interpreted as server acceptance.

## Evidence

Focused TDD reproduction before the original implementation:

```text
expected "vi.fn()" to be called 1 times, but got 0 times
```

Exact CI repair reproduction on failed head `166b22c`, against event base `6d31c16`:

```text
TypeScript LOC ratchet failed: oversized legacy files may not grow.
```

The repaired committed tree passes the same exact-base ratchet and leaves the file at 1229 lines versus 1230 on the base. Complete affected test files also pass:

```text

Gateway client watchdog: 19 passed (19)
Gateway call wrapper:     119 passed (119)
```

Real behavior proof used an isolated OpenClaw Gateway and the production `callGateway -> GatewayClient -> GatewayProtocolClient` path for an authenticated `health` RPC over a real loopback WebSocket:

```text

Callback ran before response resolution: true
Callback intentionally threw: yes
Request still resolved successfully: yes
```

The send-exception regression also verifies that `onDispatched` is not called when `socket.send` fails and that pending request state is cleaned up.

```text
Scoped lint: passed

```

target.title: fix(memory-lancedb): make table initialization atomic
target.body:
Closes #105680

## What Problem This Solves

The bundled LanceDB memory plugin checked whether the `memories` table existed and then created it in a separate operation. Two OpenClaw processes initializing the same database could both observe the table as absent, race during creation, and fail startup with a duplicate-create error.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the existing fast path for an already-present table, but make the absent-table path use the LanceDB 0.30.0 atomic `existOk` create mode. This keeps concurrency ownership in the database dependency, avoids a filesystem lock that would not fit remote storage URIs, and keeps schema-row cleanup idempotent.

The regression test starts six independent Node processes against one fresh LanceDB directory and requires every process to complete initialization successfully. The same scenario fails against the previous implementation.

LanceDB documents that `existOk: true` suppresses the existing-table error in create mode and ignores the losing caller supplied data: https://lancedb.github.io/lancedb/js/interfaces/CreateTableOptions/

## User Impact

Gateway and worker processes can initialize the same memory-lancedb store concurrently without intermittent duplicate-create startup failures.

## Evidence

Final-head validation:

- Candidate head: `4e1bc84e3e1`; rebased onto `origin/main` at `652266b8b6c`.
- Production diff after the current TypeScript LOC ratchet: `12 additions / 13 deletions`; the legacy production file no longer grows.

### Standalone concurrent-process behavior proof

Environment: macOS arm64, Node 24.15.0, exact `@lancedb/lancedb@0.30.0`, one fresh temporary local LanceDB directory. This proof ran outside Vitest. The temporary driver started six independent Node processes; each imported the production `extensions/memory-lancedb/index.ts` module and called `testing.createMemoryDb(dbPath, 4).count()`.

Pre-fix control: the same final-head snapshot with only `{ existOk: true }` removed while retaining the test access hook:

```text
initializer 2: failed (1)
initializer 3: failed (1)
initializer 4: failed (1)
initializer 5: failed (1)
initializer 1: failed (1)
initializer 6: ok
Error: Table memories already exists
before_exit=1
```

Final head:

```text
initializer 5: ok
initializer 1: ok
initializer 3: ok
initializer 6: ok
initializer 4: ok
initializer 2: ok
tables: memories
rows: 0
after_exit=0
```

The final table is usable, all six initializers return successfully, and the temporary schema row is removed.

### Tests and gates

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/memory-lancedb/index.test.ts extensions/memory-lancedb/memory-lancedb.concurrent.test.ts` under Node 24.15.0 — 2 files and 126 tests passed.
- `check:changed` passed conflict markers, the TypeScript LOC ratchet, attributions, extension export guards, duplicate coverage, dependency pins, and formatting. Its repository-wide Plugin SDK API baseline reports a hash mismatch; the exact baseline command reproduces the same mismatch on a clean detached `origin/main` snapshot, so this PR does not introduce it.
- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` — passed.
- Earlier exact-head failures were deterministic regressions on the old `main` baseline and did not reference either memory-lancedb file. The current `main` repair at [`2c95bd2387c`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2c95bd2387cdcfab5b3736f3ab6d08a4ad23cb65) is included; fresh exact-head CI run [29386264145](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29386264145) passed with 46 checks green, including `openclaw/ci-gate`.

Remote Testbox delegation was unavailable because the installed Crabbox binary is 0.16.0 while the current flow requires 0.22.0 or newer. The proof above is secretless local execution, and GitHub CI remains the remote verification lane.

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

target.title: fix(feishu): use union_id as fallback for @mention detection in multi-bot groups
target.body:
## Problem

Fixes #40768

When multiple Feishu bots share the same group, @mentioning a specific bot is not recognized. The bot logs `message in group ... did not mention bot` even though it's correctly mentioned.

## Root Cause

Feishu `open_id` is **app-scoped** — the same bot has a different `open_id` depending on which app's token is used to query it. Confirmed by querying the same message with two different bot tokens:

```
# Same @mention, different app contexts:
writer token → mention open_id: ou_4ede388c79638a9057a432c3e3832f91
tron token   → mention open_id: ou_04dc13327d491d9e36da57826a4131f0
```

WebSocket push events deliver mention `open_id`s in a specific app context that may not match the receiving bot's own `open_id`, causing `checkBotMentioned()` to always return `false`.

## Fix

`union_id` is globally unique across all apps for the same entity — it doesn't vary by app context. This PR:

1. Fetches `union_id` alongside `open_id` from `bot/v3/info` at startup
2. Stores it in a new `botUnionIds` map in monitor state
3. Passes it through to `checkBotMentioned()` as a fallback
4. Matches mentions by `union_id` when `open_id` doesn't match

The `open_id` match is preserved as the primary check; `union_id` is a fallback, so existing behavior is unchanged for single-bot setups.

## Files Changed

- `types.ts`: add `botUnionId` to `FeishuProbeResult`
- `probe.ts`: extract `union_id` from `bot/v3/info` response
- `monitor.startup.ts`: propagate `botUnionId` through `FeishuMonitorBotIdentity`
- `monitor.state.ts`: add `botUnionIds` map with proper clear/delete
- `monitor.account.ts`: store/clear `botUnionId`, pass to `handleFeishuMessage`
- `bot.ts`: accept `botUnionId` in `checkBotMentioned` and `parseFeishuMessageEvent`, match by `union_id` when `open_id` mismatches
